On the vampier end of the spectrum, Voloshyna expects black cherry to take off this season. “It looks rich on winter skin tones and feels more interesting than a classic red,” she says. Compared to cherry on its own, the purple-leaning shade is a great alternative for those who want something that feels more wintry without being holiday-specific. It’s also a particularly pretty color for a micro French tip — another trend Voloshyna predicts will be big.

Liquid Silver

With toe rings back in the mix, it only feels right to match your pedicure to your jewelry. “I think we’re moving beyond the soft glazed finishes and into something a little more bold, almost like your toes have been dipped in molten metal,” says Russell, whose go-to “liquid silver” polish is Nails.INC’s Mirror Chrome Nail Polish in Silver Served.

For a fun contrast, you can also add some dainty nail art on top, like tiny polka dots or thin stripes. “There’s something so unexpected about mixing softer, feminine details with a futuristic look,” Russell says. “It’s the perfect balance of playful and edgy.”

Tomato Red

Tomatoes may be out of season at your local farmer’s market, but as a source of nail inspiration, they’re surprisingly ripe. “We’re so used to retiring our bright colors once fall rolls around, but I think that seasonal rule is becoming less relevant, especially for a pedicure,” says Russell. Look for a vivid red with a slightly orange undertone, like China Glaze’s Flame-Boyant Nail Lacquer — it not only looks fresh, but it also “warms up the skin,” according to Russell.

Cobalt Blue

Another color to brighten up your winter pedicure rotation? Cobalt, which Russell calls “a power blue.” Though it typically calls to mind Mediterranean summers and glistening oceans, “there’s something so striking about a saturated blue against winter’s more muted wardrobe,” she says.

Voloshyna is also a fan of electric cobalt for the colder months, nothing that it “gives toes personality without being too loud.” In other words, think of it as the happy medium between neon and navy.

Bedazzled Pedis

For a matchy-matchy moment between your hands and feet, Estrada suggests going all in on bedazzled nail art. He sees the big toenail as “a compact canvas for miniature jewelry-inspired artwork,” whether that means a cluster of tiny crystals, a few pearls, or gemstones paired with metallic detailing. Even a single rhinestone accent can dress up an otherwise plain pedicure.

If you are going the maximalist route, though, one thing to keep in mind: You’ll want to stick to flatter embellishments that won’t press against your winter boots, Estrada adds. Save the three-dimensional designs for nights when you’re breaking out your open-toed heels.

Emerald Green

When you think of green this time of year, your mind probably goes straight to Christmas trees — but deep emerald is a different story. “It’s a more refined alternative to brighter holiday greens, with deeper undertones that make it feel elegant rather than seasonal,” says Wei.

Go for a cat-eye polish, and the vibe becomes “the velvet upholstery of an extravagant European palace,” as Estrada puts it. In other words, less Christmassy, more opulent.

item.title: An iPhone 18 Pro Picture Is Honored On 'Time’s Top 100 Photos List
item.description: Jimmy Chin's iPhone 18 Pro photograph was previously featured at the "What Holds Us" exhibition prior to being honored by 'Time.'
item.dc:creator: Alexis Morillo
item.content:encoded:
It’s that time of year for reflection. Time’s Top 100 Photos do just that, celebrating the best that 2026 had to offer. Among the honorees on the list this year is Jimmy Chin, who took a photo with an iPhone 18 Pro.

Chin, an Academy Award-winning director and National Geographic photographer, was one of the first photographers to shoot with the new Apple device’s camera, and he brought it along to Bugaboo Provincial Park in Canada, where inspiration struck. The resulting photo premiered in New York City in September as part of the “What Holds Us” exhibition, curated by Kathy Ryan, the former director of photography at the New York Times Magazine.

The exhibit featured photos exclusively shot on the iPhone 18 Pro, exploring the people, places, and ideas that connect us all. Along with Chin’s work, photos by fellow artists Alex Prager and Jack Davison were also included. While Chin’s work focused on natural landscapes, Prager shot vibrant lifestyle scenes, and Davison created high-contrast black-and-white images. The photograph that Time chose to honor captures Chin’s climbing partner of 25 years, Conrad Anker, summiting a mountain.

“What I was after was that intersection: human ambition in pursuit of awe and wonder, set against a landscape that was here long before us and will be here long after. Out there you are reminded how small you are. That has always put things in perspective for me, and I hope it does for whoever is standing in front of the picture,” Chin said of the image.

By using an iPhone, Chin said the experience shooting felt even more intimate. “A production puts something between you and the person in front of you — gear, crew, the apparatus of a shoot,” he says. “Working this way there was no apparatus. It was just the two of us, which is the only condition under which that kind of ease shows up in a frame.”

The What Holds Us exhibition will be open for visitors in London at the Saatschi Yates Gallery at 14 Bury St. You can stop by to check it out from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Dec. 4 or between Dec. 5 - 13 from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

item.title: 10 Best New Books To Read In November 2026
item.description: From sports romances to friendship stories, here are the best books of November 2026.
item.dc:creator: Sophie Fishman
item.content:encoded:
With Thanksgiving fast approaching, the hustle and bustle of planning menus, booking travel, and feasting with your family can feel overwhelming. But what’s better than taking some “me time” with a good read?

Fans of literary fiction have plenty to enjoy. Louise Kennedy, author of the critically acclaimed Troubles-era novel Trespasses, returns with Stations, a novel that charts a friendship over 25 years. Kit de Waal’s latest novel, Sweet Pea, celebrates the small moments of love and kindness that make up a human life.

Over on the sports-romance front, things are heating up. For anyone with a Las Vegas Grand Prix-sized hole in their heart, Crash Into You, Simone Soltani’s forbidden F1 romance, is sure to get your engines revving. And if you’re still riding the high of the Valkyries’ win, Zakiya N. Jamal’s fake-dating WNBA romance will keep you in the spirit.

Whether you’re cooking a turkey or just ordering takeout, here are Bustle’s best books of November.

Stations by Louise Kennedy

Out Nov. 3. In a small town in County Kildare, Ireland, two outsiders become fast friends. Red is from an influential family with a proclivity for trouble and Róisín’s family has recently relocated from the north amid The Troubles. Ultimately, the pair’s connection wanes when an incident sends Red running for England. Years later, visiting her estranged father and his new family in London, Róisín reunites with Red in an attempt to restore what they once shared.

How to be Less Useful by Priyanka Mattoo

Out Nov. 3. In a culture obsessed with efficiency, author-filmmaker Priyanka Mattoo dares to ask a radical question: What if we relaxed? It’s part memoir, part self-help, as the author/filmmaker documents how she unwound her identity from people-pleasing and perfectionism, learned to be more present, and ultimately, actually enjoyed the life she’d once painstakingly optimized.

Clear Water by Gabrielle Lucille Fuentes

Out Nov. 3. Recently divorced Alma Figueroa said she would never return to her hometown, Brewer, Wisconsin, but something has pulled her back. All over town in the woods and on roads, locals have been seeing girls dressed in white who disappear without a trace. Perplexingly, none of these girls match the description of the young women who have gone missing in years past. As Alma begins investigating, she begins to uncover answers to questions around her sister Kayla’s death years before.

 -

Sweet Pea by Kit de Waal

Out Nov. 3. An immigrant to the United Kingdom from St. Kitts, 29-year-old Paulette is on the precipice of the life she’s always wanted: a stable job; a marriage with her long-term partner, Denton; and a baby. When a sudden tragedy strikes, grief-stricken Paulette has a child, Bird, with Denton’s best friend. Later, as a single mother, a child the same age as her son unexpectedly enters her life — one who calls her sweet pea, just like her grandmother in St. Kitts used to do.

Crash Into You by Simone Soltani

Out Nov. 10. Formula 1 driver Zaid Yousef is finally getting back to the races after last season’s catastrophic injury. Ava Farahani is also looking for her place in the world, as rumors in the press have forced her to leave her job in F1 marketing. Although the two have admired one another from a distance over the years, they know a connection would be forbidden — Ava is the daughter of the principal of Zaid’s rival team. But when an unexpected preseason encounter leads to a positive pregnancy test, the two decide to take it on together.

Mr. Disappear by Virginia Trench

Out Nov. 10. Online dating catfisher Mr. Disappear has ruined the lives of countless victims, gaining their trust before disappearing with everything they own. After connecting on a True Crime sub-Reddit, three women from three different walks of life join forces to take him down once and for all.

Uprising by Tahmima Anam

Out Nov. 17. On an island off the coast of Bangladesh, a group of children bear witness to their mothers being bought and sold by a brutal madam named Amma, knowing that one day, they will succumb to the same fate. When a new woman, Kusum, is trafficked to the island by her own family, the girls watch as their mothers — initially skeptical of her beauty and education — come to respect her unrelenting spirit and fierce resistance. Led by Kusum, the women incite a revolution that will change all of their lives forever. Uprising is a finalist for the Orwell Prize for Political Fiction.

Two Can Play That Game by Zakiya N. Jamal

Out Nov. 17. Sex-positive influencer Chelsea has never been a sports fan, but an encounter with Adrienne “AD” Daniels, the 6-foot-4 star of the New York Rebels, might change her mind. AD, for their part, has never been able to commit to a relationship. With their reputation putting brand deals in jeopardy, they make a proposition: Chelsea should pretend to be their girlfriend for the remainder of the season. When Chelsea and AD’s fake connection starts feeling real while convincing fans and friends alike of their romance, it puts into question everything they’ve worked to build.

Tiger’s Mouth by Lucy Tan

Out Nov. 17. When Jack Chen, the eldest son of two caterers, lands a prestigious internship at tech company K.O. Systems, he’s prepared to do whatever it takes to succeed. Then his world shifts when he strikes up a friendship with fellow intern, Jack Owens, the son of the company’s billionaire founder. As the pressures of the competitive environment build around them, however, their relationship morphs into something far more ruthless.

Long Wave by Daisy Johnson

Out Nov. 24. As a toddler, Ori was found alone and stranded on a remote English island. Growing up, she was kept in the dark about her earliest years. Now, decades later, she’s given birth to her own child and is increasingly plagued by a deep-seated sense of doubt. Unraveling and losing touch with her surroundings, Ori spends her sleepless nights traveling back to the island through her memories in search of her mother.

item.title: Booked, Busy, & Staying Well: How CVS Makes Taking Care of Yourself During the Holidays Easier
item.description: Between holiday parties, endless errands, and cold and flu season, your wellness routine deserves a spot on your calendar.
item.dc:creator: BDG Studios
item.content:encoded:
For some reason, the universe decided that the most wonderful time of the year should also be the time that too many of us are waking up with a scratchy throat. But you’ve got plans. Between Friendsgiving, office parties, family gatherings, and a packed social calendar, nobody has time for a week spent in bed blowing your nose.

Unfortunately, during the busiest time of the year, taking care of yourself can quickly fall to the bottom of your to-do list.

Fortunately, staying on top of your wellness routine doesn't have to be a production. At least with CVS Pharmacy in your corner, you can cover the self-care activities to help support your wellness routine. A one-stop shop offering seasonal vaccinations, vitamins, cold and flu essentials, and everyday necessities? Now that’s a holiday miracle.

So before you RSVP to another cookie swap or volunteer to host a dinner party, consider these four ways to put your well-being on the calendar, too.

The Most Important Holiday RSVP? Your Flu Shot

You can RSVP "maybe" to your coworker's ugly sweater party, but your annual flu shot deserves a more definitive answer. According to the CDC, nearly everyone ages six months and older should get vaccinated against the flu each year, making it one of the smartest additions to your pre-holiday checklist.

Luckily, CVS Pharmacy makes it easy to find information about seasonal vaccinations, whether you're stopping by your local pharmacy or visiting CVS.com. You can make an appointment for your flu shot, or drop in impromptu when you’re restocking the medicine cabinet. Think of it as one more errand you can cross off before your calendar reaches critical mass.

And because even the most carefully laid plans can't guarantee a sniffle-free season, consider keeping a CVS Combo COVID-19 + Flu A/B Antigen Test on hand. Designed for adults and children ages two and up, the at-home test delivers results for COVID-19 and influenza A and B in just 15 minutes. Because playing detective with your symptoms is one holiday mystery nobody asked for.

Give Your Wellness Routine The VIP Treatment

When your schedule is packed with late nights, early mornings, and a suspicious number of cheese boards masquerading as dinner, your everyday routine could probably use a little extra attention.

Enter CVS Women's Multivitamin Gummies, which support daily nutritional needs and come in an adorable new heart shape with mixed berry flavor. CVS also offers Men's Multivitamin Gummies. Consider this a small act of self-care that doesn't require booking a facial or blocking off your entire Sunday.

And while we're discussing the basics, let's talk hydration. Between the holiday cocktails, endless errands, and running around town, keeping a drink within arm's reach is never a bad idea. Well Market Electrolyte Max Zero in Strawberry Flavor makes it easy to replenish electrolytes on the go.

With vitamins, beverages, and everyday grocery essentials all available at CVS, supporting your wellness routine doesn't have to mean adding three more stops to an already overbooked day.

Restock Your Wellness Products

While you can't always control when a cold strikes, you can control whether you’re prepared for the occasion.

First up: CVS Ibuprofen Pain Reliever & Fever Reducer, which temporarily relieves minor aches and pains from headaches, the common cold, and fever. The 200 mg tablets also come in new recyclable aluminum bottles, giving your medicine cabinet a practical little upgrade.

Then there's CVS Non-Drowsy Maximum Strength Tussin DM, a raspberry-flavored liquid medicine that helps relieve coughs and loosen chest congestion for adults and children ages 12 and up. And because a scratchy throat has never improved anyone's holiday experience, CVS Wild Cherry Flavor Throat Drops are another useful addition to your seasonal stash.

With a wide range of CVS Store Brand OTC products available in convenient formats and value sizes, stocking up is refreshingly straightforward. Just remember to follow label directions and consult a healthcare professional as appropriate.

Sometimes The Best Holiday Plans Are No Plans

Hot take: Not every December evening needs to be an “on the town” affair. Sometimes the ultimate festive act is declining an invitation, putting on your softest sweatpants, and spending an uninterrupted evening on the couch. Especially when you're feeling under the weather.

For those nights, the CVS Ultrasonic Dual Mist Humidifier is a welcome addition to your winter setup. With warm and cool mist options, quiet ultrasonic operation, and easy-to-adjust settings, it adds moisture to dry indoor air while you settle in for a much-needed night of doing absolutely nothing.

And if the thought of venturing outside sounds about as appealing as another mandatory office party, CVS has you covered there, too. With convenient same-day delivery through CVS.com, you can stock up on wellness essentials without leaving the house. CVS also offers prescription services for the whole household, including your four-legged family members.

Plus, many eligible health and wellness purchases may qualify for FSA/HSA benefits, and ExtraCare members can access additional savings deals.

Because the holidays are supposed to be fun, not an endurance sport. And with CVS making it easier to take care of yourself, you can spend less time stressing over the little things and more time enjoying the season.

Meet all your busy holiday season needs at CVS.

*Product prices and availability may vary in-store and online.

**CVS Pharmacy locations provide flu vaccinations to persons as young as three years of age; some restrictions apply.

item.title: The Biggest Winter 2027 Makeup Trends, According To Pros
item.description: Experts reveal winter 2027's biggest makeup trends, from cold girl blush and stardust eyes to wine-stained lips and candlelit skin.
item.dc:creator: Emma Stout
item.content:encoded:
There’s a fine line between giving yourself enough time to get ready and giving yourself too much. On one hand, you can relish the luxury of being able to turn up some music and mix yourself a cocktail. On the other, when you’ve finished your entire makeup with 45 minutes left to spare, you’re liable to start getting creative. Perhaps you decide it’s the perfect time to try graphic eyeliner for the first time. Next thing you know, you’re reaching for a bright red lipstick, and before you know it, you start thinking maybe Alix Earle was right: Maybe this is too much for a little bar in New Jersey.

Well, on the bright side for anyone prone to getting carried away with their makeup: Winter is arguably the best time to do it. “There’s something about the holiday season that makes people want to experiment a little more,” says celebrity makeup artist and Ciele founder Nikki DeRoest. “People are embracing more glamour, whether that’s a bold lip they wouldn’t normally wear or a wash of shimmer across the eyes.”

With all the parties and dinners to go, it makes sense — but experimenting doesn’t have to mean trying every technique at once. In fact, “sometimes it’s just about doing one thing a little differently,” DeRoest says. Think a swipe of berry blush across the bridge of your nose, a flick of burgundy eyeliner, or a few spiky lash clusters along your lower lash line.

Ahead, the winter 2027 makeup trends to try whether you’re rushing out the door or taking your time, straight from the pros.

Stardust Makeup

Some believe fate is written in the stars — and they may be worth looking to for your next beauty inspiration, too. Meet: stardust makeup — aka sparkly shadows, shimmery cheeks, and pearlescent lips. “Instead of doing a full frosted eye and lip like we did in the early 2000s, I love choosing one feature and letting that be the focus,” says DeRoest.

For a more “sophisticated” take on stardust eyes, celebrity makeup artist and founder Lisa Eldridge recommends “softly sculpting with a taupe or neutral shade before pressing a little icy shimmer onto the center of the lid.” And don’t feel limited by silver: Pink and champagne can be just as dazzling.

You can also dust a little shimmer onto the inner corner, says celebrity makeup artist Ash K. Holm — just be intentional about the placement. “Rather than carrying shimmer all the way up to the brow bone, keep it concentrated where the light naturally catches.” To finish, she suggests pairing it with defined lashes and understated lips to “create a beautiful contrast in textures.”

“Cold Girl” Blush

Even if you’re not a fan of cold weather, there’s something to be said about the rosy flush that comes after a brisk walk in January. Fortunately, you can recreate the look with a little berry, plum, or burgundy blush.

“The key is that the color should look as though it’s coming from within the skin rather than sitting on top of it,” says Eldridge. To get that effect, she suggests starting with a small amount of blush, really working it into the skin, and building up the color gradually.

Another pro tip to make it look more effortlessly windburnt? “Bring a tiny bit across the bridge of the nose for that natural winter flush,” says DeRoest.

Candlelit Skin

According to DeRoest, people are ditching overly perfected makeup looks in favor of something lighter and more luminous. “People are becoming more comfortable with letting their natural skin show through,” she says. In other words, think hydrating skin tints over full-coverage foundations this season. (Your winter dry patches will thank you, too.) The goal: a softly illuminated complexion, as though you're permanently standing in the flattering glow of a candle.

To keep your base looking fresh, apply a thin layer of tint, then go back in with concealer where you need extra coverage, according to DeRoest, who recommends ciele’s tint & PROTECT SPF 50+.

For the finishing touch, Holm suggests strategically powdering around the nose, chin, and center of the forehead, while leaving the high points of the face luminous. “The goal is polished, red carpet-worthy skin that still looks like skin.”

Soft Smoky Eyes

If stardust lids feel angelic, smoky eyes are the devil on your other shoulder. And this winter, the devil’s all in the details: brown, plum, pewter, even burgundy shadows. “They add depth without feeling quite as harsh as black,” says DeRoest.

For an easy way to try the look, apply a cream shadow all over your lids and soften the edges with a small brush. “I love adding a little extra color close to the lash line for definition,” says Eldridge, who recommends her Seamless Glide Cream Shadow Stick in Smokey Amethyst. And don’t worry about being too precise — in fact, “it looks better when it’s a little undone,” DeRoest adds.

Wine-Stained Lips

’Tis the season for matching your lipstick to your glass of red wine. Rich merlot and burgundy shades are back in rotation — but unlike the red lips of holidays past, this year's version looks like it’s already survived a kiss (or two) under the mistletoe.

“I love the idea of a statement lip that doesn't necessarily look overly precise or formal,” says Eldridge. To get that blurred finish, apply the color to the center of your lips, then blend it outward with your fingertips, according to DeRoest.

Bottom-Lash Energy

Forget ghost lashes. This winter, the pendulum is swinging in the complete opposite direction — from top to bottom.

“I think people are really starting to embrace false lashes, particularly on the under-eyes,” says celebrity makeup artist Jamie Greenberg, whose go-tos are from Dark Swan of Denmark. For a wide-eyed doll effect, try a few individual clusters along your lower lashes, or use a full strip for a bolder look. Or simply pile on the mascara until your bottom lashes get a little bit of that spidery separation (in the best way).

Unlaminated Brows

For anyone with slickback fatigue: Winter hair trends are getting looser, and the same goes for brows. “I think laminated brows have had their moment, and they’re being traded for something softer and more natural,” says Greenberg.

Not that you should retire your brow gel — but instead of combing every hair straight up, try brushing your brows more outward, following the direction they grow. (It’s “browlick”-friendly, too.)

One & Done Details

Looking to zhuzh up your everyday makeup for a holiday party? No need to overhaul your entire routine. “Sometimes the smallest detail can completely change the feeling of a look,” says Eldridge.

Her picks? Metallic accents in the inner corners of the eyes, a glossy statement lip paired with otherwise minimal makeup, or an unexpected eyeliner color like burgundy. That shade can be particularly flattering, too: “It can make brown eyes appear lighter while intensifying green and blue eyes,” according to Holm. Her current favorite is Victoria Beckham’s Satin Kajal Liner in Bordeaux.

Whatever you choose, “it doesn't need to be complicated,” as Eldridge puts it — or intimidating, for that matter. Just commit to a single detail and have fun with it.

item.title: Kerry Washington's Guide To High-Low Gifting This Holiday Season
item.description: Kerry Washington shares her favorite high-low holiday gift ideas, from Cécred hair oil to budget-friendly picks on Google's Holiday 100 list.
item.dc:creator: Rachel Chapman
item.content:encoded:
Finding the perfect gift takes serious strategy. You have to hit that sweet spot between practical and unique without blowing your budget — a balancing act Kerry Washington has down to a science. Her cheat code? Keeping tabs on the trends. Literally.

According to the Animals star, the real magic lies in taking an affordable, of-the-moment staple and tailoring it to your recipient. “For example, if you look at Google’s Holiday 100 list, kitten heels are massive,” she tells Bustle. “Everybody wants them, but depending on the person you’re getting them for, is it a patent leather kitten heel or a leopard print kitten heel? There's so many ways of personalizing that gift for the person you know well.”

Spotting trends is second nature for Washington, who cemented her fashion-icon status as Scandal’s Olivia Pope. For the rest of us with 47 browser tabs open, it helps to see what other people are searching for most online. That’s where the Holiday 100 list comes into play, curating the most sought-after items in beauty, tech, style, and more for easy gifting inspo.

While the annual gift guide is great for kicking off your holiday shopping, Washington also narrowed down her personal favorites — especially when it comes to budget-friendly finds that feel splurge-worthy. Below, she shares her go-to picks along with her best advice for high-low gifting this season.

You’re a queen at power dressing, so what’s your No. 1 tip for balancing investment pieces with budget-friendly gifts?

I like to mix up my fashion. My wardrobe is high-low. The pieces that are closest to my skin are the ones where quality matters. It’s most important that I’m comfortable, and then I can play around with those bigger ticket pieces, like a bag or a jacket that I use again and again.

What is the one gift category where you always splurge, and where is the budget version secretly just as good?

Splurge on anything that’s health and wellness related, like the Cécred hair oil or a lymphatic face brush. You really want those things to be quality, because that’s investing in your health and wellness. And then, you can have a little more flexibility and fun with the more kitschy gag gifts and toys.

If you invest in quality beauty tools, they’ll last you a long time.

Yes, and they save you money on treatments at the dermatologist and time on makeup because your skin looks so good you don’t need it.

Looking at Google’s list, you’ve also highlighted the Uniqlo Pointelle Cardigan. What is your styling advice for making an affordable staple like that feel more luxurious?

Layering. It’s always going to be about layering. With that cardigan, we paired it with this very cute sequined skirt. It could also be worn with a really beautiful silk camisole. You could combine it with a jacket or a blazer over it, or a really beautiful silk scarf. When you layer an item like that, it adds to the luxury of it.

Another cozy staple you selected is the Pilates resistance set, and we know you’re a massive devotee. Since athleisure has completely taken over our closets, what is your top tip for taking a workout look from a morning session straight to a chic holiday brunch?

One of the things that’s easy about Pilates is you can do it barefoot or with socks, so you can wear a dress shoe to class and look fabulous on your way in and on your way out. It also really comes down to the layering again and even color-blocking. Keeping my athleisure in neutral tones that match well with different setups and add-on pieces really helps.

Are there specific layers you like to pair with your performancewear to make it look high fashion?

A blazer is always great. I noticed that those silk scarves are on the list this year, which was so funny for me. I just thought that’s perfect because you can really do so much to dress up a look with a beautiful scarf. This time of year, a blazer and boots is a no-brainer. Leggings would look one way with sneakers and a totally different way with a boot.

You picked both an LED facial mask and the Instax Mini 13 from the list, but if you absolutely had to choose one to receive, would it be the high-tech luxury item or the nostalgic one?

The red light.

What’s your go-to white elephant strategy? Are you a hilarious gag gift person, or is the low-key useful budget find more your thing?

I like a useful gift. In today’s day and age, we all have so much stuff that finding a gift they’re actually going to use is very important to me.

Finish the sentence: The best gifts are the ones that make you feel...

The best gifts are the ones that make you feel inspired.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

item.title: Rob Lowe Discusses His New Documentary & 4 Favorite Books
item.description: Rob Lowe joins Bustle’s One Nightstand interview series to share his favorite books, including Joan Didion’s ‘The Year of Magical Thinking.’
item.dc:creator: Charlotte Owen
item.content:encoded:
In One Nightstand, celebrity readers and writers join us at the blond in 11 Howard to discuss some of their favorite books, allowing us to learn about their tastes and lives in the process.

Rob Lowe has been famous for more than four decades, but even starting out in the early 1980s meant he was too late for the days when the press could be kept on a leash — an era vividly captured in David Niven’s memoir The Moon’s a Balloon, one of the four books Lowe has chosen to discuss today. “The press would take orders,” he says. “I have a friend who was in the Blue Angels in the ’60s. He told me a story about being at a party. JFK invited the Blue Angels because he was an aviation enthusiast, and [a famous actress] apparently walked into the party nude, but with a mink and was like, ‘The president will be down in a few minutes, boys.’ And no one said a word.” He pauses. “By the way, for the record, I have no idea if that story is true, but that was directly from my friend who flew with the Blue Angels.”

Lowe may have come of age in a different media cycle, but his career speaks to his ability to stay ahead in an industry obsessed with what’s new and what’s next. His new documentary, Rob Lowe: The Outsider, spotlights the vicissitudes of the 62-year-old’s life, from his personal battles and eventual sobriety to his fight to break through as a young actor. “I’m so interested in the new James Bond reveal,” he says. “Robert Pattinson got it, and he’s the best. Like duh, Robert Pattinson, hello, sure… When I came up, it was like Tom Cruise and Patrick Swayze and Kevin Bacon, and they’re like your frenemy. You want them to win, but not at a cost to you.”

The documentary is one half of a Netflix double-header for Lowe, who also appears in the streamer’s festive rom-com In a Holidaze as an eccentric honorary uncle. Being the veteran on set made for a full-circle moment with his younger colleagues. “I remember when Hal Holbrook, the great character actor, was on The West Wing for a week,” he says. “I just wanted to hear every story from him. Now I’m sitting there and there’s Maddie Ziegler and all the kids going, ‘Tell me about this and that.’ I’m like, ‘I’m that guy. I’m that guy.’”

Surely top of the list were questions about St. Elmo’s Fire, the 1985 cult classic in which Lowe’s performance as Billy Hicks, opposite Demi Moore and Emilio Estevez, turned him into a star. A sequel is in the works. “We’re trying to get the script right,” he says of a possible reunion. “In St. Elmo’s Fire, my character has got his sax slung across his back [at the end] — not in a carrying case, of course — and he’s getting on the bus to New York. So he literally gets to New York almost a year before the sax solo is completely removed from every pop hit. Overnight, no sax solos. So my thing is he gets there and gets one big sax solo in Billy Ocean’s ‘Caribbean Queen,’ and then it’s curtains and [he] has to figure out what to do.”

Keep reading to discover four of Lowe’s favorite books.

'The Killer Angels' by Michael Shaara

Bookshop -

'The Moon's a Balloon' by David Niven

World of Books -

'The Year of Magical Thinking' by Joan Didion

Bookshop -

'What It Takes' by Richard Ben Cramer

Bookshop -

Lowe’s first selection is The Killer Angels by Michael Shaara, a Pulitzer Prize-winning fictional account of the Battle of Gettysburg. “It’s soaring, emotional, inspirational, and patriotic,” he says. “That it really happened is amazing, but more than anything, it’s the subject matter and the prose.”

Throughout the book, Confederate leaders feel doubtful about Robert E. Lee’s choice of military tactic. Ultimately, many defer to the General’s authority, choosing not to raise red flags. Lowe likens that mentality to working with Peter Bogdonavich, whom he describes as “the General Lee of movie directors” on the 1988 film Illegally Yours. He was initially skeptical of the script but decided to trust the legendary director’s expertise. “I was like, ‘I don’t know. I kind of like the script, Lee…’ But I was young,” he says. “This is an analogy you never saw coming — Peter Bogdanovich versus Robert Lee and a rom-com versus the Civil War.”

Ultimately, the film was a box-office flop, grossing around $259,000 against a reported $13 million budget. “Like Lee and Gettysburg that day, I was decimated by the loss of that movie because the General definitely sent me on Pickett’s Charge,” he says. “The number one thing that anybody in life should do, but particularly as a creative, is trust your instincts.”

Lowe is also a fan of Gettysburg, the 1993 film adaptation featuring his West Wing co-star Martin Sheen as Robert E. Lee — except for one thing. “Worst beards you’ll ever see. I’m telling you, it’s Saturday Night Live-level beards,” he says. “Tom Berenger, I love him. He’s a great actor. But that beard. It’s like they took muskrats and just soldered them to their faces.”

The actor’s love of history runs in the family. “My son, Matthew, who's a military history major, recommended it to me,” he says. “When he got married three weeks ago, he walked down the aisle to ‘Ashokan Farewell.’”

His second pick is actor David Niven’s 1971 memoir The Moon’s a Balloon. Lowe says he turned to the book for inspiration while writing his first memoir, Stories I Only Tell My Friends. “It delivers on all of the things a memoir has to, but a lot of them don’t, particularly when they’re written by celebrities,” he says. “It has to be honest, unflinching, no b*llsh*t, warts and all, authentic. It has to name names. He has to give the people what they want, but in a way that’s not gratuitous and in a way that’s not taking shots or going for a pull quote.”

His third choice is The Year of Magical Thinking, Joan Didion’s 2005 memoir recounting the year following her husband’s death while her daughter Quintana was critically ill. “I love Joan Didion. Probably if I have to pick one, she’s my favorite writer,” he says. “Incidentally, I used to see her every morning at a drop-off in Malibu. My brother, Chad, was in Quintana’s class. I was too young to know her but I knew she was some kind of writer, and she had the famous Stingray.”

Throughout the book, Didion describes keeping mementos from her loved ones who have passed. Lowe says his family is less sentimental. “My version of it is, ‘Oh, well, I really need to keep this ill-fitting crew jacket from John Irving’s Hotel New Hampshire adaptation film that I made. It doesn’t really fit me, but for my kids,’” he says. “And then they’re like, ‘Nah, not interested.’"

During this interview, Lowe learned that Didion briefly mentioned him in her 1988 essay Insider Baseball. “What? I got mentioned by Joan Didion? You’ve made my day. She knew who I was!” he says. “That’s up there with having a star on the Walk of Fame.”

His final pick is What It Takes: The Way to the White House, a nonfiction account of the 1988 presidential election from Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Richard Ben Cramer. The author follows each politician from the moment they announce their candidacy through the general election. The theme that ties together the six men is persistence, a trait Lowe takes to heart.

“I’m just naturally resilient. My self-image is of those old toys that we grew up with — the inflatable clown, you punch it in the nose and it would go wink, and then it would slowly come back up,” he says. “If you don’t have that, then you are very easily one of the many people who have a couple of movies and are gone and never come back. You have to be able to keep coming back, and a lot of people aren’t built that way.”

item.title: 'Dig': Antonia Thomas On Playing Clare, Career, & Friendship
item.description: Antonia Thomas opens up about playing Clare on Peacock's delightful new archaeologist comedy 'Dig.'
item.dc:creator: Grace Wehniainen
item.content:encoded:
Never has the workplace comedy looked so aspirational as it does in Peacock’s Dig. Co-created by Parks and Recreation’s Amy Poehler and Michael Schur — and based on Kate Myers’ novel Excavations — the new Peacock series (out now) takes place at an archaeological dig in Greece. Sure, it’s dirty and sweaty, and plenty goes wrong. But it’s also a place where four women unearth a surprising friendship and a career-making discovery they’d like to keep secret from their overbearing boss.

Antonia Thomas plays Clare, a buttoned-up conservator planning her wedding, but coming to terms with the fact that her perfectly curated life isn’t totally serving her. As the actor tells Bustle, the real love story is the one between the colleagues — brought to life by Poehler, Thomas, Geraldine Viswanathan, and Fina Strazza.

“They’re all doing their own thing,” Thomas says over Zoom from a cottage in the English countryside, where she was celebrating her 40th birthday in early November. “They’re all completely different, and they’re all at different phases of their lives, but all realizing that they’re questioning where they are and not sure if what they’re doing is the right thing. It’s just really beautifully written in that they all manage to learn something from one another.”

Thomas is learning a lot about herself too. The Good Doctor and Misfits alum has been flexing new acting muscles over the past year, genre-hopping from vacation drama Two Weeks in August to detective series Tommy & Tuppence. In Dig, she continues to prove her versatility.

“That kind of comedy world was something new for me, and that was a challenge,” Thomas says. “It just feels like an exciting jumping-off point where I’m like, ‘OK, I want to take on more things that I don’t know yet how to do.’”

Below, Thomas opens up about karaoke with the cast, her hopes for a second season, and what’s next.

Your chemistry as a cast is amazing. Can you tell me about a time behind the scenes that you felt that energy?

At the beginning of the series, we’re introduced relatively separately [on screen] — so it was a while before we all got to be together as girls. That happened for the first time at the dig site, and we were looking down at the statue like, “Oh, my God.” This unlikely girl gang.

And then, at the very end of the shoot, we were in Italy, all staying in the same hotel, and we got to meet for dinners. The hotel had this amazing piano player, and we ended up doing karaoke with him. It was this beautiful old masseria, and we were the only ones there. And he only had the songs he knew how to play, so we all managed to find one and blasted it out. I did Tina Turner’s “Simply the Best.”

What did you envision Clare’s relationship with Gary to be up to this point? It feels like she’s been taking a path in life that’s very “don’t rock the boat, don’t do anything crazy.”

Clare’s big emotional arc is realizing that she doesn’t need to please her mother, and her engagement to Gary is very much a product of going, “I’m at the stage in my life where I really ‘should’ be married now. I should have kids. I should be... whatever.” And Gary’s there in the place where she spends a lot of time, because she does want to work on the dig site. And so she’s like, “That guy will do. He’s nice. I can mold him.” He’s a lovely guy. He’s just not really right for her.

It was so nice that Clare stands up to her mom. Can you talk about that mother-daughter dynamic?

Oh, my God, it was so fun. Noma [Dumezweni] is the most incredible actress, and I have been such a fan of her work from afar for a really long time. We have a lot of friends in common from the British scene. Instantly on meeting, we were chatting, chatting, chatting. We both had a really clear idea of what their lives had looked like — which is, she thinks she’s being a good mum by setting her daughter on the right track. But she’s just so preoccupied with the world that they live in and what everybody thinks that she’s never made room to actually listen. She still loves her daughter. She’s probably not going to change as a person, but she can learn to loosen that up a little bit.

I love that at the end Clare’s like, “I’m going to India. No itinerary.” Is there a time that you’ve done that?

This industry can be a little bit like that. Sometimes you get opportunities, and you’re like, “There’s the safe choice, and then there’s the one that really scares me, and I don’t know if I can do it — but I’m just going to do it anyway.” That choice of going for the path less trodden, not playing the role that you know you can do, I try to apply that to my job.

Is there a specific genre or role that you imagine?

For me, it’s all about the writing — if the character is well-drawn and interesting. I’d love to do a really serious piece of drama. I’d also like to do something quite genre-y. I love a really good intellectual horror or a thriller. But really, I’m open to any challenge.

Should there be a Season 2, what would you love to see for Clare?

There’s so much fun to find in the nuance of this female friendship, and where that can go. Seeing them leaning into the new freedom of the choices that they’ve made would be really interesting.

I would love to see Clare really letting loose. The comedy of her trying to do that and embrace it, versus her personality, and trying to find that sweet spot of what feels true to her, would be really fun to watch.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

item.title: The 1 Hunger Games Press Tour Look Mckenna Grace Couldn't Pull Off
item.description: Mckenna Grace’s stylist, Molly Dickson, reveals the viral 'Hunger Games' scene they couldn't recreate on the press tour, plus hidden Easter eggs you missed.
item.dc:creator: Alyssa Lapid
item.content:encoded:
If you thought Mckenna Grace’s dedication to The Hunger Games maxed out when she brought a binder of book notes to the Sunrise on the Reaping set, you clearly haven’t heard about her press tour mood boards. Over the past few weeks, the actor turned every red carpet into a Panem fashion tribute, serving up looks packed with deep-cut references and Easter eggs only superfans like herself could clock.

Though she left the binder at home this time around, Grace *did* show up to her fittings armed with visual inspiration. “Mckenna was very, very clear about what she wanted from the beginning,” her stylist, Molly Dickson, tells Bustle. The vision? Full-blown method dressing, a red carpet approach Dickson doesn’t typically take: “Her excitement and passion for the idea was honestly contagious, and that made me even more excited to bring it all to life for her.”

And deliver they did. Her homages ran the gamut, with Dickson transforming Grace into everyone from Rue to Lucy Gray. And since her character Maysilee Donner was the original owner of the mockingjay pin, Katniss was obviously a pillar reference — Grace even bookended her press run with Katniss’ unforgettable wedding gown *and* mockingjay dress. They didn’t stop at onscreen nods, either, pulling IRL inspo from the OG cast’s own red-carpet archives.

“As much as I wanted to make every one of Mckenna’s ideas happen, Peeta’s rock might be the one that got away.”

Still, there is one truly unhinged look Grace wishes they could’ve pulled off: Peeta’s infamous rock camouflage. If you’ll recall, Grace is a certified Team Peeta stan who used to make fan edits growing up. Naturally, Josh Hutcherson’s character was at the top of her vision board — particularly *that* scene.

“Mckenna actually really wanted to recreate that iconic moment,” Dickson says. Unfortunately, executing it proved to be a challenge. “We explored the idea, but I just couldn’t find a way to translate it into a fashion look that felt elevated rather than costume-y,” she says. “As much as I wanted to make every one of Mckenna’s ideas happen, Peeta’s rock might be the one that got away.”

Ahead, Dickson spills on the Easter eggs fans missed, the late-night text that sparked an archival Céline hunt, and the hardest look to bring to life.

Congratulations on the press tour! Was there an Easter egg fans might have missed on the carpet?

One of the most hidden ones was the white dress she wore to SiriusXM ahead of the premiere. It’s a reference to Johanna Mason’s white gown in the Capitol propaganda portraits for The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 1.

I actually remember seeing this white structured vintage Givenchy dress in 2011, and I knew it would be the perfect nod to that character.

You don’t typically lean into literal method dressing quite like you have on this tour. What made Mckenna and SOTR the exception to your usual rule?

It’s a very collaborative process with all my clients. My job as a stylist is to take my client’s vision and bring it to life. If they don’t necessarily have a clear vision, then it’s my job to help them discover and create one.

The most important thing is staying true to who my client is. In this case, method dressing felt so authentic to Mckenna and her excitement around this project that it made perfect sense to fully embrace it.

Mckenna famously brought a binder of book notes to set. Did she come to your first styling fitting with a master spreadsheet of Hunger Games references?

She didn’t come with a binder, but she definitely had Pinterest boards and mood boards ready for me, which I absolutely love. I’m such a visual person, so whenever a client comes to me with references or ideas, I get so excited. It gives me a great understanding of what they’re envisioning and makes the creative process that much more collaborative.

Mckenna knew the Hunger Games world so well, and I loved how much thought she had already put into what she wanted to reference. My job was to take those ideas and figure out how to translate them into fashion moments that still felt like her, rather than costumes.

You’ve referenced some of Katniss’ most elaborate looks. Apart from those, what was the most difficult homage to pull off?

One of Johanna Mason’s looks — the lumber look. Mckenna texted me one night and said, “I need to be a tree.” I was completely confused at first because I had no idea how to turn a tree into a fashion moment without it feeling too literal or costume-y.

After a major research rabbit hole, we eventually came across this incredible Céline by Phoebe Philo piece that almost resembled wood. We reached out to practically every vintage rental house and dealer we could think of, and after all that searching, we ended up finding the archival Céline piece on The RealReal of all places.

Method dressing walks a very fine line between chic fashion homage and looking like a costume. What was your personal rule for keeping these looks editorial so Mckenna was the one wearing the dress rather than the dress wearing her?

Fashion always has to come first. No matter how perfect a reference might be, if the look isn’t flattering or doesn’t feel like Mckenna, then it’s not the right look.

That’s one of the biggest challenges with method dressing. You can have the most incredible reference, but bringing it to life in a way that still feels fashionable and true to your client’s personal style is a completely different story. You can’t get so attached to a concept that you lose sight of the person wearing it.

At the end of the day, I want people to see Mckenna looking incredible, and then discover the clever reference behind the look. Not the other way around.

As a lifelong fan, Mckenna must have had a pinch-me moment during fittings. Which look made her the most emotional when she zipped it up?

Mckenna was just so incredibly grateful and genuinely excited about every single premiere look. We did multiple fittings for each gown, and somehow her excitement never faded. Every time she put one on, it felt just as special as the first time.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

item.title: My Boyfriend Is Into Kinky Sex & I’m Not. Am I Boring?
item.description: Ever since I found some kinky toys my boyfriend used with his ex, I can't help but feel insecure about our vanilla sex life.
item.dc:creator: Sophia Benoit
item.content:encoded:
Q: My boyfriend and I are pretty open about our past experiences with sex and relationships. I know how many people he’s been with, how he lost his virginity, and even how he used to deal with performance anxiety. All fine!

We’re moving in together, and when I was helping him pack up his things, I found a box way under his bed with bondage rope, a ball gag, and a butt plug. He sincerely apologized, said they were from his last relationship, and promised that he hadn’t kept them on purpose; he just hadn’t gotten around to throwing them away. (I believe him. He's kind of messy.) He told me that he was fully “vanilla” before he met his ex, she got him into it, and he wound up loving it. For five years, pretty much their whole sex life was kinky in some way or another.

He knows that I’m not remotely adventurous in bed — no judgment at all, it just doesn’t appeal to me — and now I worry that he secretly thinks our sex life is not just boring, but even bad. Is something crucial missing for him?

Since I found the box, I’ve felt super insecure in bed, and he’s been initiating less often than he used to. On one hand, the drop is understandable (he’s been working long hours, the apartment hunt was stressful), but we’ve been talking about getting engaged next year, and I worry that it’s finally hitting him that he probably won’t have kinky sex ever again. He promises me that he loves our sex life and says he’s fine giving that up, but should I really trust that? Should he have to give up what he really wants? Is that going to come back to bite us?

A: In my work as a sex and relationships columnist, I have interviewed loads of people about their sex lives; I’ve discussed virtually every kink imaginable and what makes it titillating and fun or inconvenient and unrealistic. I’ve spoken to people in their 60s who have been married for decades and people in their 20s who are in polycules. There’s one question I always ask: What’s the best sex you’ve ever had?

You know what the unifying theme has been? It’s not ropes or plugs! It’s intimacy.

A few people have divulged a particularly erotic fling, but by and large, they say their hottest encounters have been with a partner they care about and feel close to. Above any position or specific sex act, they emphasized connection.

So please believe me when I say that while your boyfriend might genuinely enjoy kink, there is also very much a world in which he is perfectly fine never having it again if that means getting to have sex with you for the rest of his life.

Also, believe me when I tell you that kinky sex can be “meh,” too. The same person who wants to try the wheelbarrow might discover that they can only come when they’re on top. Even if someone loves getting spanked with a paddle, they might occasionally find their mind wandering back to the tax form they need to file this week. You don’t have kinky sex to manufacture arousal or connection; you have kinky sex because you want to enhance arousal with someone you’re already connected with. (Even if that connection is meeting seven minutes ago at the BDSM dungeon.)

Just because your boyfriend has enjoyed kink in the past doesn’t mean he views your sex life as a step down. When I am 74, I will likely think fondly back to playing beer pong in college. In no way does that mean I wish I had upended my life and turned pro. Not to get too ecclesiastical, but to everything there is a season, even ball gags.

Could he occasionally fantasize about butt plugs or tying you up? Sure. Those can be solo pursuits. Is it possible that he’ll eventually miss kinky sex? Yes. There is also a chance he could develop a shellfish allergy. There is a possibility that you are offered a dream job in Cleveland. Hopefully, you’ll be able to talk about whatever life throws you and navigate it as needed. But that only works if you set up the skill of talking about your feelings around sex in a mature, healthy way now.

You guys need to have another conversation, one where you get really vulnerable about this insecurity. Tell him how his recent dip in initiation makes you feel. Together, brainstorm what might make you feel more desired, pursued, and secure.

It’s OK to crave reassurance. It’s normal to have needs and healthy to express them. That does not make you “unreasonable” or “needy” or whatever other loaded term your brain comes up with. If you can’t go to your partner for a little extra love and comfort, who can you go to? They shouldn’t be the only way you address your self-doubts, of course, but they should be willing to defend you even to your own mind.

I do think that this problem points to a larger issue, which is that you trust your own anxieties more than you trust your partner.

When people talk about the importance of trust in relationships, it’s not just about fidelity. It’s about taking your partner at their word. You don’t believe your boyfriend when he says he wants a lifelong sexual relationship, despite ample evidence that he does. (He’s moving in with you! He wants to marry you!) Beyond that, you don’t trust that he would voice his concerns to you if he did have them.

Why is that? Has he had a hard time opening up to you about his relationship concerns in the past? Did your ex keep secrets from you? Do you compare yourself to his ex in other areas of your life, too?

Most of us are guided by our insecurities from time to time, and those moments often are painful and disappointing in hindsight. I find that when I act from a place of insecurity, I often end up not just assuming the worst about myself, but also about other people — that they will judge me harshly as I judge myself. Assuming that someone is looking down on you and then not believing them when they say otherwise is just not a great way to interact, especially with those you love the most.

Also, consider that your desires might evolve over time. Someday, you might want to try wax play or a threesome. There are all kinds of “yes, no, maybe” lists that catalogue various sexual acts — from sex in a blindfold to acting like furniture for another person to sit on — that you and your partner could use to assess potential overlapping interests. Many let you answer beyond a yes or no, too. They’re a nice way to have open-ended conversations about sex.

Remember that every part of your life could be different with someone else. Maybe there are even parts that could be better with another partner. You could date someone who doesn’t set and snooze seven alarms every morning. Perhaps you occasionally miss your ex’s sister, whom you were really close to. None of that is an indication you’re with the wrong person.

Let’s say you decide to have your honeymoon in Madeira. That doesn’t mean that you dislike all other possible destinations on Earth and what they might offer, but above all, you can’t wait to see Portugal.

Your boyfriend has picked you. He’s excited to have a future with you. Please believe him. It will make life much, much easier on you both.

It’s A Pleasure appears here once a month. If you have a sex, dating, or relationship question, fill out this form.

item.title: November 24, 2026's Full Moon Most Affects These 3 Signs
item.description: These three zodiac signs will be dealing with major twists and turns under November's full Beaver Moon, according to an astrologer.
item.dc:creator: Nina Kahn
item.content:encoded:
Thanksgiving week feels extra festive this year, as it’s delivering this month’s chain-breaking and mind-expanding full moon. Rising on Nov. 24 in the fast-talking and frenetic sign of Gemini, this lunation shines a light on the way people think and express themselves, emphasizing the nuances in your communication style and general philosophy. There’s a sense of unpredictability and excitement in the air with this one, but there’s also some tensions at play, too. If you’re one of the signs most affected by the Nov. 24 full moon, you’re likely to feel it all — the good, the bad, and the chaotic.

November’s full moon happens to be a supermoon — meaning it’s peaking closer to the earth than usual and will therefore appear bigger and brighter — and it’s traditionally dubbed the Beaver Moon. It’s named for the fact that beavers tend to ramp up work on their shelters during this time of year, building their lodges and dams in preparation for the fast-approaching winter. While the airy and mutable lunation on Nov. 24 is more thematically aligned with mental matters than physical security, it can still help you prepare for all that’s yet to come by encouraging you to think outside the box and open your mind to unforeseen possibilities.

The reason for this is that the full moon will be closely bonded to maverick planet Uranus, which is the cosmic ruler of shocking changes and futuristic innovations. Under this influence, you’ll want to expect the unexpected. Because the full moon is in quizzical Gemini, this will be especially notable when it comes to processing information — both intellectually and interpersonally. Conversations could take wild turns, and some connections could come as a serious surprise. In fact, you may even come to some conclusions that defy your usual conventions or traditions. It’s time to break out of your usual box and interrupt the patterns that are holding you back from aiming higher and further.

The electrifying buzz of this Uranian lunar conjunction can be thrilling, but the full moon will also be locked into a frustrating and hot-headed T-square with aggressive planet Mars, turning up the desire to act impulsively and hastily. Gemini zodiac energy can lean chaotic, and having the full moon be so wrapped up with Uranus is most certainly amplifying that element of things. However, all this tension with Mars makes everyone more likely to see that chaos manifesting in their reactions and defenses, so it’s important to check yourself before you wreck yourself. Breaking a cycle and operating outside the status quo is one thing, but bringing volatile behaviors into the mix is only going to make you feel less in control.

Change is on the horizon, especially if you’re one of the zodiac signs most affected by Nov. 24’s full Beaver Moon. Read on to find out if you’re one of them.

Gemini (May 20 - June 19)

You’ve been exploring your unconventional side this year, so you’ve probably picked up on a lot of things about yourself that make you feel out of sync with the status quo. This full moon in your sign brings an opportunity to accept these quirks and differences, and to start integrating them into the way you move through the world and connect with others.

You may have some unexpected feelings come up that make you question your beliefs or relationships — but that’s not a bad thing! Feelings aren’t facts, but they can serve as helpful clues that show you who you are, what’s important to you, and where your relationships stand. Practice honoring whatever comes up for you and expressing it openly.

Leo (July 22 - Aug. 21)

You’ve been turned inside out over the past month, growing in all sorts of new ways while also letting go of so much that no longer fits your storyline. You’re at the tipping point of a serious breakthrough, but this full moon is asking you to look at your current state through a more objective lens. Set the personal aside for a moment and consider yourself as part of something larger. Are your actions contributing to a cause or mission that matters? When you visualize the future, are you taking an active role in creating what you see?

Your visions don’t exist in a vacuum, and this full moon wants you to give your goals some context. Connection is the key to understanding right now, so consider the ways in which you’re creating community and giving your intentions meaning.

Sagittarius (Nov. 21 - Dec. 20)

It’s your season, but it’s the close people in your life that’ll be grabbing most of your attention under this full moon. Unexpected dynamics in relationships could emerge now, causing you to look at others — as well as yourself — in a different light. Additionally, conversations about commitments or agreements could wind up taking some surprising turns, inspiring you to lay out some unconventional conditions or suggestions.

As the saying goes, it takes two to tango — but that’s no simple statement when you’re talking about two ever-evolving, complex, emotionally-driven humans. There’s not just one way to be in relationship with someone, so lower the fences around your paradigms and be open to new ways of connecting.

For more, check out your tarot reading.

item.title: Anna Camp On ‘2:22,’ A ‘True Blood’ Reboot, & Her Theater Rituals
item.description: Anna Camp, starring in ‘2:22: A Ghost Story’ off-Broadway, talks about her theater routines, what she’d want to see in a ‘True Blood’ reboot, and more.
item.dc:creator: Christina Amoroso
item.content:encoded:
When Anna Camp signed on to star in Danny Robins’ thriller play 2:22: A Ghost Story at the Lucille Lortel Theatre, she didn’t expect to have ghost encounters of her own. “I had one onstage the other day,” she says. “I saw, no joke, a white orb of light facing upstage [moving] from stage right to stage left, all the way to stage right in front of my face. My brain started to rationalize: ‘Did something fall from the ceiling?’ And I became very alert.”

Camp became convinced it was the ghost of the theater’s namesake, actor-producer Lucille Lortel. (“We know the Lortel is haunted by Lucille herself,” she says. “And I’ve heard the lore and the tales about it.”) In 2:22’s next scene, there’s a fire onstage, and on this particular night the flames went off early while Camp had her back to it. “I think Lucille was warning me to stay alert so that I didn’t back myself into the fire. I told everybody backstage, ‘I think she was protecting me,’” she says. “And then Richard [Abel], our house manager, was like, ‘Oh, this is the time of year where she starts to show up — when it gets to be a little chillier.’”

It’s a fitting experience for 2:22. The show follows a young couple and new parents, Sam (Finn Jones) and Jenny (Jasmine Cephas Jones), the latter of whom hears odd noises coming from their daughter’s bedroom every night at 2:22 a.m. while Sam is away on business. Jenny begins to believe that their new home is haunted, and when Sam returns, she convinces him and their two friends to stay up until 2:22 to prove that the supernatural occurrences are indeed happening. Camp plays Lauren, a booze-loving psychotherapist and college friend of Sam’s who, like Sam, is initially skeptical of Jenny’s claims.

“She’s trapped between the rational and the irrational thoughts,” says Camp. “She’s going back and forth in this conflict that she’s playing throughout the play, being torn and then on top of it, and dousing herself in alcohol to not feel things.”

The suspense and jump scares that ensue make for a collective audience experience similar to seeing horror films in a movie theater — and Camp would know, having starred in Scream 7 along with other spooky or supernatural projects like True Blood and You. “It’s just really cool to hear the audience react,” says Camp. “It’s so much fun to be scared in a group of people because somehow you feel safer.”

On owning the stage:

My first Broadway play, I was really young. Mike Nichols directed it, and I was acting onstage with Morgan Freeman and Frances McDormand. I was like, “What am I doing here?” I would be talking to him, and he’d just casually be talking about being in Glory or Driving Miss Daisy. I would have so many butterflies. He would just keep talking and talking, and then it would be time for his cue and he would just walk out onstage casually and the place would erupt in applause — right? Because it’s Morgan Freeman.

On the roles she’s drawn to now:

I’m 44 now, and there’s so much stress and pressure on a woman to look young and be young and be an ingénue — “Don’t play a mother yet until you really have to” and all that stuff. And I’m like, “Well, those are the meatier roles.” I’ve grown a lot as an actor and as a woman. So much has changed in my life that I feel more comfortable with who I am. And it’s exciting to get to come onto a stage more fully realized as an adult, without all that self-consciousness and fear, and see how that translates to being in front of an audience eight shows a week. I feel really excited to get out there, so much more than I used to, when the nerves would sort of overtake the confidence. Now, I’m like, “Oh, I’m a woman.”

On stage door fans:

It’s really nice to be able to see that my work is affecting people in a positive way, because when you’re in Los Angeles, you don’t get that fan reaction, that one-on-one time. And sometimes you’re in this bubble of, like, “Is my work reaching people? Do people really respond to it?” It’s also been really cool to see fans of Pitch Perfect coming. A girl wanted me to write “Aca-excuse me” on her Playbill because it was going to be her tattoo. I go, “So wait, this is going to be your tattoo?” And she goes, “Yes, my first one.” And I went, “Oh, my God, the pressure — do you want it big or small?” And the parents behind her go, “Small.” I went over to the wall and was like, “Nobody talk to me for a second — this has to be perfect.” But she seemed really happy.

On her pre-show routines:

I like to get as grounded as possible and usually light a candle. There’s this brand Kai Rose, and I absolutely love them — it smells like roses and fills up the entire space. I’m not one of those actors who can just be in their dressing room and just go to the stage. There’s a certain stool that I have a lot of emotional moments on, so I like to go out and sit on the stool for a minute, look at the lights, and say hi to Lucille, because I feel like she’s looking out for me. And I go to her portrait sometimes and just say, “You’re beautiful, you know — thank you.”

And then we’re all backstage together. So we laugh and play music, and me and Jas riff and do our makeup together and talk about girl stuff. Jasmine and I love to play Enya — this show is scary, and your heart is racing. We’re fighting for things. We’re crying. We’re screaming a lot. So we love putting on Enya — we’re like, there’s our girl. We just vibe and chill and listen to Enya. It’s literally the best thing ever.

On her post-show cocktail hour:

I have a glass of rosé that’s waiting for me in the refrigerator, so that the minute I come off stage I can have a little sip of wine. I’m a rosé girl, and I have three bars in the West Village that I kind of rotate through: Little Owl, which is so great; Buvette, which makes an amazing dirty Tito’s martini — I was there just last night with Constance Wu, because she came to see the show, so we had a little martini moment; and then Jeffrey’s Grocery, where I do my oysters and orange wine. So when friends come, I pick one of those three spots, and we all just go and talk about the show. That’s the other beautiful thing about doing a play in New York — I’m seeing people I haven’t seen in years.

On soaking up other NYC theater:

On my day off, I stay horizontal and in bed for as long as humanly possible, and then I go see a play. It’s great. I’ve been seeing lots of plays because I don’t live in New York anymore, so I’m craving theater. It’s so nice to be in the audience and have someone else perform for me, because I’m doing it every day.

I’ve seen Other Desert Cities, which is great. Downstate — blown away. So incredibly good. What a dangerous play. I’m going to see Inter Alia on my day off, and I really want to see Much Ado About Nothing, which just opened.

On manifesting a True Blood reboot:

Sarah Newlin, the character I played, is not dead. The last time we saw her, she’s hanging up in the basement of Fangtasia, and she’s curing all the vampires. At the very end, I was just begging the writers, like, “Please make me a vampire.” So I would love to play a vampire in it and obviously get the whole cast back. Come on, let’s get Alex Skarsgård back. Anna Paquin, I love her so much.

It still has such an amazing fan base. I’ve also noticed younger people, like some Gen Zers, watching it for the very first time, which has been really exciting. They’re coming up to me even at the stage door being like, “I just started watching True Blood. I love the show. Why is it gone?”

item.title: November 24, 2026's Full Moon Least Affects These 2 Signs
item.description: These two water signs are feeling more subtle vibrations under November's full Beaver Moon, according to an astrologer.
item.dc:creator: Nina Kahn
item.content:encoded:
Sagittarius season always has a certain sparkle to it, but this year it’s off to an especially buzzy start thanks to the full moon rising on Nov. 24. Traditionally known as the annual Beaver Moon, November’s big lunation also earns itself supermoon status this year, as it’s reaching peak fullness from a relatively close distance to the earth — so it’ll appear extra large and bright in the skies. This ultra-charged lunar moment will send shockwaves through everyone’s social lives and thought processes. However, if you’re one of the signs least affected by the Nov. 24 full Beaver Moon, then it may feel more like a shallow ripple than a tumultuous breaker.

Symbolized by the cosmic archer, Sagittarius zodiac energy is about setting your aim high, looking toward faraway horizons, and shooting for the stars — so ever since Sagittarius season began on the night of Nov. 21, there’s been a heavier cosmic emphasis on these themes. However, this full moon takes place directly across the zodiac in airy and mutable Gemini, which is much more interested in its immediate surroundings and present moment. It’s less concerned with birds-eye-view perspectives and blanket philosophies and more with straight-up information. Unlike worldly and dogmatic Sagittarius, Gemini processes things in real time and changes its personal stance as needed. With that in mind, this lunation can help you see the facts without being so tied to an opinion, even if it means having to accept something that’s surprising or completely unexpected.

The unpredictability factor of this lunation comes from Uranus — the planet of sudden change and innovation — which is sitting in a tight conjunction with the full moon. Under this influence, it’ll be beneficial to think outside the box and keep an open mind. Don’t shy away from being unconventional in your approach. Your truth may not always align with the status quo, so check your preconceived notions at the door and accept the shifts in your reality. You may finally find the words needed to break out of an old cycle and level up your frequency.

Additionally, the moon will be making a beautiful lucky and powerful connection to small but mighty Pluto, which brings depth and intensity to all full moon endeavors. Change that’s been slowly brewing beneath the surface may finally reach its tipping point, pushing situations through a threshold that’s been long-building but overlooked. Under this Beaver Moon, the dams that have been holding old paradigms in place may finally start to break, resulting in greater clarity and much-needed transformations.

This is a powerful lunation, but that doesn’t have to be a bad thing. Read on to find out if you’re one of the lucky zodiac signs least affected by Nov. 24’s full moon.

Cancer (June 20 - July 21)

Some people will feel this full moon like an electric shock, but you’ll probably just feel some subtle vibrations coming from somewhere deep within you — so it’s important to quiet your mind and listen. This lunation isn’t hitting your chart as dramatically as it is for most members of the zodiac, but you’re still slowly coming to some private and internal realizations. However, they’ll be easy to miss if you don’t give yourself a chance to hear them.

Your emotional antennae might feel like they’ve been retuned to a different frequency, allowing you to pick up on feelings and intuitive hits that may not immediately make sense. Instead of trying to draw big conclusions, simply let the information you’re receiving sit and simmer. Things will start clicking into place when the time is right, so there’s no need to draw out your hypotheses just yet.

Scorpio (Oct. 22 - Nov. 20)

You’ve just come out the other side of a very heavy and transformational Scorpio season, full of retrogrades and challenging aspects — so you’ll be pleased to know that this full moon will likely feel more subtle than the last few lunations. Instead of getting plunged into any chaotic emotions or drastic actions, now is a time to consider where you’d like to set some limits and step back.

Examine your closest relationships — whether those are with people, creative projects, business endeavors, or even pieces of your own identity — but break free of the lens of what’s “normal.” If you were genuinely listening to your heart, which of these attachments are actually serving you and making sense versus which are draining your resources and becoming more complicated? This full moon brings you an opportunity to adjust your boundaries as needed, without the influence of people who aren’t involved.

For more, check out your tarot reading.

item.title: How Mckenna Grace’s Stylist Hid Her ‘Hunger Games’ Mockingjay Dress
item.description: Stylist Molly Dickson breaks down Mckenna Grace’s ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ premiere gown and smuggling those Mockingjay wings past NYC holiday crowds.
item.dc:creator: Alyssa Lapid
item.content:encoded:
Mckenna Grace closed out her The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping press tour with a literal flex. On Nov. 16, the actor hit the New York red carpet in an homage to *the* mockingjay dress — unfurling a pair of oversized Claudia Marin wings over a custom cobalt Pamella Roland gown. It was a full-on fashion moment, cementing Grace’s place in the method dressing Hall of Fame.

But behind the scenes, the effortless reveal actually required covert ops. “It was like a top-secret mission getting her out of that hotel,” Grace’s stylist, Molly Dickson, tells Bustle. They were staying at a busy Manhattan hotel with holiday crowds bustling in and out. “We strategically snuck the wings into a box in her car just minutes before she got in, so no one would realize what they were or who they were for.”

Of course, some fans had an inkling Grace would end her press circuit with the mockingjay dress. The biggest clue? Her tour opener in Paris. On Oct. 6, Grace stunned onlookers with a recreation of Katniss’ wedding gown, setting the tone for the looks to follow.

Anyone well-versed in Panem lore knows the famous wedding dress transforms into the mockingjay silhouette in Catching Fire — a cinematic metamorphosis Dickson intentionally echoed. As she explains, Grace’s press tour wardrobe was always meant to tell a full-circle story: “We realized that if we opened the tour with the wedding gown, it was only fitting to bring in the fire gown midway through and ultimately close with the mockingjay wings.”

The look was doubly meaningful, too. Beyond serving as an iconic franchise symbol, Dickson notes that the wings felt like the “perfect final chapter” because they “represent strength, transformation, and everything we were trying to celebrate through Mckenna’s fashion on this tour.”

As expected, a fashion masterplan of this level isn’t easy to pull off. And the premiere look alone took half a year of planning to execute. “I always compare [creating a custom look] to designing your wedding dress,” Dickson says, sharing that she started reaching out to designers in early May. After months of mood boards, sketches, fabric selections, and fittings, it all came down to a grueling final sprint: Crafting the wings alone required three days of nonstop work.

All that planning paid off, and seeing the final look come to life brought Dickson to tears. “When Mckenna stepped onto the carpet and spread her wings in front of all the fans, I completely lost it,” she says. “It felt like this beautiful celebration of Mckenna, the fans, and the entire journey we had been on throughout the press tour. I’ll honestly never forget it.”

item.title: Croix Bethune Shares Her Wellness Habits & NWSL Finals Thoughts
item.description: The NWSL’s Midfielder of the Year shares her wellness routine, which includes a special coffee order and go-to playlist.
item.dc:creator: Megan LaCreta
item.content:encoded:
In Chill Chat, Bustle sits down with celebrities, influencers, and athletes to talk about all things wellness, from daily routines to hacks for getting a good night’s sleep. Here, Croix Bethune dishes on the importance of recovery, setting the NWSL assist record, and facing off against her old team in the championship match.

On Nov. 21, the Kansas City Current sailed to victory under the bright lights of Audi Stadium, defeating the home team Washington Spirit 2-1. This win clinched the franchise’s first-ever NWSL Championship title. Among the Current’s starting line-up was Croix Bethune, a pre-season trade from the Spirit, who had a historic season in her own right.

The 25-year-old midfielder left finals weekend with her first championship ring and NWSL’s Midfielder of the Year Award for the second time since she joined the league in 2024.
